approved: Family Assistance and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2013
Families, Housing, Community Services and Indigenous Affairs

Supported the Family Assistance and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2013, which from 1 July 2013 reduces the baby bonus for second and subsequent children from $5,000 to $3,000 while keeping it unchanged for first children, saving $500 million to $600 million over four years, and defended the Schoolkids Bonus of $410 per primary and $820 per high school student, which has injected $588 million nationally and helped 16,100 families in his electorate of Blair, alongside the tax-free threshold rising from $6,000 to $18,200.

Opposed the bill's cut to the baby bonus for second and subsequent children from $5,000 to $3,000 from 1 July, which the government expects will save $505.9 million over four years, argued the policy was originally introduced in 2002 to counter Australia's fertility rate falling below 1.9 against a 2.1 replacement rate, and cited Sweden's experience, where family-friendly policies briefly lifted fertility above two children per woman before it fell to 1.52 by the end of the century.

Supported the Family Assistance bill, defending the $5,000 baby bonus for a first child and $3,000 for subsequent children as reasonable given lower costs for later children, contrasted this with the New South Wales Liberal government pulling $1.7 billion out of education, welcomed the extension of dental care to all children from July 2014, and praised the Better Futures, Local Solutions program, operating in 10 regions including part of her electorate where one in four families is jobless, for supporting young mothers to complete their education.

Opposed the Family Assistance bill's baby bonus cut as a half-billion-dollar tax grab targeting families with a stay-at-home parent to help offset the budget deficit, noting Labor's last budget surplus was delivered in 1989.

Supported the bill as a sustainable family assistance measure, including reducing the baby bonus for second and subsequent children to $3,000 from 1 July, while defending Labor's broader family payments, childcare rebate, pension and employment measures.

Announced amendments to replace the baby bonus with family tax benefit loadings, including $2,000 for a first child and each child in a multiple birth and $1,000 for later children, while changing paid parental leave eligibility and reducing family assistance claim periods from two years to one year.

The speaker argued that the bill's cuts to the baby bonus, reducing it from $5,000 to $3,000 and later abolishing it in favour of a lower family tax benefit loading, harm families and undermine the policy's goal of boosting Australia's fertility rate. Specific figures cited include the baby bonus reduction from $5,437 to $5,000, then to $3,000, and the replacement offering $2,000 for the first child and $1,000 for subsequent children.
